topicTitle: Storing Data: Variables (let, const, var Intro)

lessons.title: Declaring Variables with let and const
lessons.description: Learn how to store values using the let and const keywords — the two modern ways to declare variables in JavaScript.

sections.heading: What is a variable?
paragraphs: A variable is a named container that holds a value. Think of it like a labeled box: the label is the variable name, and the box stores whatever you put inside. Variables let your program remember data so you can use it later — without variables, every piece of information would vanish after one line of code.

sections.heading: Why variables matter
paragraphs: Without variables, you could not do anything useful in programming. You need variables to: remember a user's name, keep score in a game, store a price for calculation, track whether a checkbox is checked. Every program, from a tiny script to a massive app, stores and retrieves data using variables.

sections.heading: The three keywords: let, const, and var
paragraphs: JavaScript gives you three keywords to create variables: let, const, and var. In modern JavaScript, you should use let and const. The old keyword var still works but has confusing behavior — we will cover why to avoid it in lesson 1.3.3.

sections.heading: Declaring with let
paragraphs: let creates a variable whose value can be changed later. Use let when you know the value will be updated — like a score counter, a timer, or a user input that changes.

sections.heading: Declaring with const
paragraphs: const creates a variable that cannot be reassigned after its initial value is set. Use const by default — it tells anyone reading your code that this value is not meant to change. Only switch to let when you genuinely need to update the value.

codeExamples.heading: Creating variables with let and const
explanation: let score = 0; creates a variable called score and puts the number 0 inside it.
The second line score = 10; replaces the old value with 10. That is what let allows — changing the value later.
const playerName = "Alex"; creates a variable that holds the string "Alex". Because it uses const, trying to set playerName = "Sam" later would throw an error.

codeExamples.heading: Different data types in variables
explanation: Variables can hold different types of data. A string is text wrapped in quotes, a number is numeric, and a boolean is either true or false.
You do not need to declare the type — JavaScript figures it out from the value you assign. This is called dynamic typing.

practice.task: Create a let variable called temperature and set it to 30. Print it, then reassign it to 35 and print again. Then create a const variable called pi set to 3.14 and print it.
hints: Create const pi = 3.14; and print it. Notice you cannot reassign a const.
practice.note: Try reassigning the const variable to see the TypeError you get.

keyTakeaways: let creates a variable that can be reassigned — use it when the value will change.
const creates a variable that cannot be reassigned — use it by default.
Variables store different data types: strings, numbers, booleans, and more.
Always declare variables with let or const — never write bare assignments.
lessons.challenge: Create a variable lives set to 3 using let. Write code that subtracts 1 from it, then prints the result. Finally, try the same with const — what error do you get?

lessons.title: Variable Reassignment & Identifier Naming (camelCase)
lessons.description: Understand how variable reassignment works, learn the rules for naming variables, and adopt the camelCase convention that every JavaScript developer uses.

sections.heading: Reassignment with let
paragraphs: When you use let, you can update the variable's value at any time by using the = operator again. The old value is replaced — the variable only holds one value at a time. This is called reassignment.

sections.heading: Why const cannot be reassigned
paragraphs: The whole point of const is to signal that a value should stay the same. If you try to reassign a const variable, JavaScript throws a TypeError. This protects your code from accidental changes to values that should be fixed.

sections.heading: Valid identifier rules
paragraphs: Variable names (identifiers) must follow these rules:
list: Can contain letters, digits, underscores (_), and dollar signs ($)
Must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign (not a digit)
Are case-sensitive — name and Name are two different variables

sections.heading: The camelCase convention
paragraphs: In JavaScript, the standard naming style is camelCase: the first word is lowercase, and every following word starts with an uppercase letter. For example: firstName, totalPrice, isStudent. This makes multi-word names easy to read at a glance.

codeExamples.heading: Reassigning a let variable
explanation: temperature starts at 20. The second assignment replaces it with 25.
The third line reads the current value (25), adds 5, and stores the result (30) back. This is a common pattern: read the current value, compute something new, store it back.

codeExamples.heading: camelCase naming in action
explanation: Notice how camelCase makes multi-word names readable: firstName clearly means "the first name".
Boolean variables often start with is, has, or can to signal true/false — like isStudent and hasPermission.
Descriptive names beat short ones. courseCount is much clearer than cc or n.

practice.task: Create a let variable balance set to 100. Subtract 30, then add 50. Print the final value. Then create variables using camelCase for: a user's email, their age, and whether they are an admin.
hints: For camelCase names: let userEmail = "...";, let userAge = 25;, let isAdmin = false;
practice.note: Try to create a variable called 2ndPlace. What happens? Variables cannot start with a number.

keyTakeaways: Use let when you need to reassign a variable's value later.
Variable names must start with a letter, underscore, or dollar sign — not a number.
camelCase is the standard JavaScript naming convention: firstName, totalPrice.
Use descriptive names. userAge is better than a.
lessons.challenge: Write a small "bank account" script: create variables for account holder name, balance, and whether the account is active. Deposit 500, withdraw 200, and print the final balance. Use camelCase for all names.

lessons.title: Why var Should Be Avoided in Modern Code
lessons.description: Discover the pitfalls of the old var keyword and understand why let and const replaced it in modern JavaScript.

sections.heading: What is var?
paragraphs: var is the original way to declare variables in JavaScript, dating back to 1995. It still works today, but it has behavior that surprises even experienced developers. Modern JavaScript introduced let and const specifically to fix these problems.

sections.heading: Problem 1: var is function-scoped, not block-scoped
paragraphs: Variables declared with var ignore if blocks, for loops, and {} blocks entirely. They are scoped to the nearest function, or to the global scope if declared outside any function. This means a var variable declared inside an if block is accessible outside it — which is usually not what you want.

sections.heading: Problem 2: var allows redeclaration
paragraphs: With var, you can declare the same variable name twice in the same scope without any error. The second declaration silently overwrites the first. This is a common source of bugs — you might accidentally reuse a name and overwrite an important value without realizing it.

sections.heading: Problem 3: var is hoisted to the top
paragraphs: JavaScript moves all var declarations to the top of their scope before running any code. This means you can use a var variable before the line that declares it — it will just be undefined instead of throwing an error. This makes bugs harder to track because the code runs without crashing, but with wrong values.

codeExamples.heading: var leaks outside blocks
explanation: Even though message is declared inside the if block, it is accessible outside. That is because var ignores block boundaries.
With let, this would throw an error — which is the safer behavior. let keeps variables confined to the block where they are declared.

codeExamples.heading: var in a loop — a classic bug
explanation: With var, there is only one i shared across all iterations. By the time the setTimeout callbacks run, the loop has finished and i is 3.
With let, each iteration gets its own j — so each callback captures a different value (0, 1, 2).
This is one of the most famous JavaScript bugs, and it is the main reason let was introduced.

codeExamples.heading: var redeclaration and hoisting
explanation: The second var x = 20 silently overwrites the first. No error is thrown — you might not even notice the overwrite.
Because of hoisting, console.log(name) on line 1 does not crash. It prints undefined because the declaration was moved to the top but the assignment stays in place. This is confusing and error-prone.

practice.task: Try these in the console: (1) Declare var x = 1; inside an if (true) { } block and log x outside it. (2) Redeclare var test = 1; and then var test = 2;. (3) Log a var variable before declaring it.
hints: For (1): if (true) { var x = 1; } console.log(x); — notice it works outside the block.
For (2): Both declarations succeed. The second overwrites the first silently.
For (3): console.log(y); var y = "hello"; — you get undefined, not an error.
practice.note: Now try the same experiments with let instead of var. The behavior is very different.

keyTakeaways: var is function-scoped — it ignores if blocks, loops, and other {} boundaries.
Variables declared with var can be redeclared in the same scope, which causes silent overwrites.
var declarations are hoisted to the top of their scope, allowing confusing use-before-declaration.
Always use let or const in modern JavaScript. Only encounter var in legacy code.
lessons.challenge: Find or write a loop that uses var and setTimeout. Observe the bug. Then fix it using let. Explain in your own words why the fix works.

lessons.title: Basic Mutability Concepts with const
lessons.description: Understand that const prevents reassignment but not mutation — and learn how to properly freeze objects and arrays.

sections.heading: Reassignment vs mutation
paragraphs: There is a crucial difference between reassignment (changing what a variable points to) and mutation (modifying the contents of what a variable points to). const prevents reassignment, but it does not prevent mutation. A const object can have its properties changed, added, or removed.

sections.heading: const with objects and arrays
paragraphs: When you create an object or array with const, the variable stores a reference (a pointer) to that object in memory. const prevents you from pointing the variable at something new, but you can still reach through the reference and change the object's properties or the array's contents.

sections.heading: Making objects truly immutable
paragraphs: If you need an object that cannot be changed at all, use Object.freeze(). This locks all existing properties so they cannot be modified, added, or deleted. Note that Object.freeze() is shallow — nested objects inside a frozen object can still be changed unless you freeze them too.

sections.heading: Immutability as a best practice
paragraphs: Instead of changing existing data, create new objects with the updated values. This pattern (called immutability) makes your code easier to debug because the original data stays untouched. It is especially important when working with frameworks like React, where detecting changes relies on new references.

codeExamples.heading: const prevents reassignment, not mutation
explanation: user.age = 26 modifies the object through the reference — const allows this because the variable still points to the same object.
user = { name: "Sam" } tries to point user at a completely new object — this is reassignment, which const blocks.
The key insight: const protects the binding (the variable's connection to a value), not the value itself.

codeExamples.heading: const with arrays
explanation: colors.push("blue") adds an element to the array — this is mutation, and it works even with const.
colors[0] = "yellow" replaces the first element — also mutation, also allowed.
Trying to assign a completely new array to colors fails because that is reassignment.

codeExamples.heading: Using Object.freeze() for true immutability
explanation: Object.freeze() returns the same object but locks all its properties. Any attempt to modify, add, or delete a property is silently ignored (in non-strict mode) or throws an error (in strict mode).
This makes settings truly immutable — not even const alone provides this guarantee.

codeExamples.heading: Immutability pattern: create new instead of mutating
explanation: The spread operator (...) copies all properties from original into a new object, then overrides score with 150.
The original stays untouched. This pattern is the foundation of immutable data in JavaScript.

practice.task: Create a const array of three numbers. Push a fourth number, change the second number, then try to reassign the entire array. Note which operations succeed and which fail.
practice.note: Now create an object with Object.freeze() and try to modify a property. What happens?

keyTakeaways: const prevents reassignment but does not prevent mutation of objects or arrays.
Objects and arrays stored in const variables can have their contents changed freely.
Object.freeze() makes an object truly immutable — properties cannot be added, removed, or changed.
For truly immutable data, prefer creating new objects over mutating existing ones.
lessons.challenge: Create a const shopping cart (an array of objects). Add an item, update the quantity of an existing item, and remove an item — all without reassigning the cart variable. Then use Object.freeze() on a cart item and try to change its price.
